title: Housing vouchers and neighborhood choice
summary: We studied a change in how housing voucher rent limits are set, and whether it affected where voucher households lived.
question: In 2018, the Small Area Fair Market Rent policy changed how rent limits were set for housing vouchers. Did that change where Housing Choice Voucher households were concentrated?
approach: Built a census-tract panel covering 2014 to 2022 using HUD housing data, then compared Dallas County with Harris County.
Used difference-in-differences with tract and year fixed effects. We also checked trends with an event study and mapped the data with GeoPandas.
Looked at voucher concentration alongside neighborhood racial composition and poverty.
takeaway: We found an association between the policy change and lower voucher concentration in the treatment area. The trends before the policy were different across the two counties, though, which makes it difficult to say how much of the change was caused by the policy itself.
limitation: HUD suppresses small household counts, and these data don’t tell us where individual households moved. Along with the differences in pre-policy trends, those gaps limit what we can conclude.
credits: Team: Lingyue Hao, He Jiang, Ammy Lin, Myla Simmons, and Anvita Suresh.
image_alt: Repository event-study chart showing estimated treatment effects by year with uncertainty intervals
image_caption: Event-study estimates from our analysis. The notebooks explain the model and how we interpreted the results.

title: Training sparse neural networks
summary: How many neural network connections do we actually need? We compared three sparse training methods on CIFAR-10.
question: We wanted to see how much we could reduce a neural network’s connections while keeping its predictive accuracy. We also compared methods that keep the same connections with methods that change them during training.
approach: Compared fixed sparse masks, Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET), and gradient-guided RigL on a CIFAR-style ResNet-20.
Trained at 90%, 95%, and 98% sparsity, using both SGD with momentum and Adam.
Compared accuracy curves and weight visualizations, and looked at how connections changed during training.
takeaway: Static sparsity was a competitive baseline in our experiments, and RigL generally did better than SET. The optimizer made a difference, too. At the highest sparsity level, the model had clearer limits on what it could learn.
limitation: We used one model family and CIFAR-10, with no data augmentation and only 15 training epochs. These results describe those runs; they don’t establish which method would work best in other settings.
credits: Team: Ammy Lin, Tonantzin Real Rojas, and Anvita Suresh. Completed for Introduction to Deep Learning at Duke University.
image_alt: Project bar chart comparing final test accuracy for static sparse, SET, and RigL training at three sparsity levels
image_caption: Final test accuracy across methods and sparsity levels. Our notebooks and paper describe the training setup.

title: Sparkify: music recommendations
summary: A music recommendation pipeline built with Airflow, PostgreSQL, and Streamlit. We used simulated listening data to test how the pieces worked together.
role: I worked on exploratory analysis, Airflow DAGs, the Streamlit dashboard, the recommendation model, and team coordination. These responsibilities were shared with teammates; the repository has the full breakdown.
question: How do we turn track metadata and listening history into recommendations that can be updated on a schedule and viewed in a dashboard?
approach: Combined public track metadata with generated users and synthetic listening events.
Used Airflow to schedule data ingestion, embedding generation, and recommendation updates, with PostgreSQL for storage.
Built a Streamlit dashboard to view the recommendations and added Python tests and workflow checks.
takeaway: The model was one part of the project. We also connected data preparation, scheduled inference, storage, and validation so the recommendations could make it into a dashboard people could use.
limitation: The listening histories are simulated, so we haven’t shown how well these recommendations would work for real listeners. We also haven’t tested the synchronous inference approach with a large user population.
credits: Team: Jordan, Aesha, Ammy, and Tonantzin. We shared work on the model, orchestration, dashboard, and testing; the repository lists our responsibilities.
image_alt: Sparkify Streamlit dashboard displaying the recommendation results table
image_caption: Our Streamlit recommendation dashboard, shown with the prototype’s generated listening activity.

title: Looking inside a four-neuron model
summary: I followed a small sentiment model from its predictions to its hidden neurons, then turned neurons off to check what changed.
role: I reproduced the starter model’s training and wrote an investigation of its activations, output contributions, and neuron ablations. The notebook builds on a team sentiment-model exercise.
question: What can we reasonably say that a hidden neuron does? I used a small model where I could inspect every allowed input and check an explanation against counterexamples.
approach: Reproduced a model with six input words, four hidden neurons, and two output scores. It used 28 training examples and four validation examples.
Compared activations across positive and negative inputs, then calculated how each neuron contributed to the difference between output scores.
Set individual activations to zero without retraining, checked all 32 combinations, and looked for examples that challenged an overly broad explanation.
takeaway: Turning off neuron 2 changed five of the 32 predictions. Its contribution pushed the model toward a negative answer, but it also activated for positive inputs. Calling it an exclusively negative detector would have missed that distinction.
limitation: This is a six-word task that ignores word order. The 32 combinations include the training data, and only four examples were held out. The findings describe one seeded toy model, not how a language model understands real sentences.
credits: Investigation by Ammy Lin, building on a team starter-model exercise for AIPI 590. The notebook explains which training results were reproduced.
image_alt: Two charts showing changes in predicted labels and output scores when each of four hidden neurons is turned off
image_caption: The ablation results saved in my investigation notebook. These cover all 32 allowed word combinations, including the training examples.

title: Building a spelling corrector
summary: A Python spelling corrector that weighs how common a word is against how likely a particular typo would be.
question: If a word has a typo, how do we choose the most likely intended word? This project combines word frequencies with an error model for insertions, deletions, and substitutions.
approach: Loaded word counts and character-level error counts to estimate word and edit probabilities.
Generated vocabulary candidates one insertion, deletion, or substitution away from the input, then ranked them using the language and error models.
Kept known words and used a deterministic ordering to resolve ties. The repository also includes tests of the corrector.
takeaway: The candidate list and the ranking model both matter. A likely correction still has to be in the vocabulary and within the edits the implementation considers.
limitation: The implementation handles single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions. It does not include transpositions or sentence context, and it can struggle with rare words and names.
credits: Repository: Ammy Lin. This is an implementation of a standard noisy-channel spelling-correction approach.

title: Streaming trip data with Kafka
summary: A local streaming pipeline that sends generated trip events through Kafka and PostgreSQL to a live Streamlit dashboard.
question: How do we get events from a running producer into a database and dashboard as they arrive? I used simulated ride-sharing trips to work through that flow.
approach: Generated trip events in Python and published them to a Kafka topic.
Consumed the events into PostgreSQL, using trip IDs to avoid inserting the same event twice.
Built a dashboard with city filters, recent trips, and summaries of fares, distances, and vehicle types. Docker Compose starts the local services.
takeaway: The project connects a producer, message broker, database, and dashboard in one local example. The repository includes a screenshot and recording of the dashboard updating.
limitation: The trips are synthetic and the system is a local demonstration. Kafka offsets and database writes are not committed as one transaction, so the example does not establish exactly-once processing or production reliability.
credits: Project repository: Ammy Lin. The producer, consumer, and dashboard are separate Python scripts.
image_alt: Streamlit trip dashboard with a city filter, recent trip table, and charts of revenue and vehicle types
image_caption: The dashboard screenshot from the repository, using generated trips.

title: How oil prices reach the gas pump
summary: We compared how crude oil price changes showed up in retail gasoline prices on the East Coast and in the Midwest.
context: Team project in econometrics and time-series analysis
question: Do oil-price changes reach gasoline prices differently across regions? We compared the East Coast and Midwest using weekly data from January 2022 through March 2026.
approach: Prepared price series from EIA and FRED, then checked stationarity and evidence of cointegration.
Estimated vector error correction models to study long-run relationships and short-run adjustment.
Used structural VAR models and impulse responses to compare how price shocks moved through the two regions. The analysis files are written in R and Quarto.
takeaway: Our reported long-run elasticities were close to 0.68 in both regions. The East Coast showed stronger cointegration evidence, while the Midwest showed larger gasoline-specific shocks. Similar long-run estimates did not mean the regional dynamics were identical.
limitation: The structural VAR uses an ordering assumption about which prices can respond within the same week. Results also depend on the sample period and model choices, so they should not be read as a current gasoline-price forecast.
credits: Team: Ammy Lin, Farnoosh Memari, Tonantzin Real Rojas, and Isaac Vergara Mercenario. This repository is a fork of the collaborative project.
image_alt: Weekly East Coast and Midwest gasoline prices and WTI crude oil prices from 2022 through 2026
image_caption: The weekly price series used in our analysis. Gasoline is shown in dollars per gallon and crude oil in dollars per barrel.

title: Modeling flood risk
summary: For this class project, we used synthetic data to compare flood-risk models and try out payout rules for parametric insurance.
role: I was the Project Manager and Risk Strategist. The repository lists each team member’s role.
question: For insurance that pays out when specified conditions are met, how do we choose rules that are understandable and reliable? We used a flood-risk example to look at that question alongside model accuracy.
approach: Compared linear regression, XGBoost, and sparse optimal decision trees using 20 features describing the environment, infrastructure, land use, and governance.
Used SHAP to examine feature importance, then tested sensitivity to reporting bias and changes in feature distributions.
Simulated tiered payout rules and compared thresholds for different stakeholder priorities.
takeaway: We compared models alongside the payout rules they might support. The simulations also let us try different thresholds depending on which stakeholder priorities we wanted to emphasize.
limitation: All of the data are synthetic. The feature rankings and payout rules are experimental, and would need to be checked against credible real-world data before being used for insurance or disaster response.
credits: Team: Lingyue Hao, He Jiang, Ammy Lin, Myla Simmons, and Anvita Suresh. Completed for IDS 705: Machine Learning at Duke University.

title: Simulating credit portfolio losses
summary: Using Monte Carlo simulation to see how default probabilities and correlations between borrowers affect a credit portfolio’s losses.
question: What happens to portfolio losses when borrowers are more likely to default at the same time? We looked at how default probabilities and correlations changed the loss distribution.
approach: Started with the public Default of Credit Card Clients dataset as the basis for the portfolio.
Used a Vasicek one-factor model, with a shared systematic factor and borrower-specific factors, to model defaults.
Simulated losses under different default-probability and correlation assumptions, then compared Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk.
takeaway: Expected loss doesn’t tell the whole story. In our simulations, changing the dependence between defaults could substantially change the tail of the loss distribution, where the largest losses occur.
limitation: The results depend on the one-factor model, the scenarios we chose, and a historical dataset. This was a classroom simulation, so it shouldn’t be read as a forecast of current credit losses.
credits: Team: Jordan Andrew, Ammy Lin, Farnoosh Memari, and Tonantzin Real Rojas. Completed for MATH 789 at Duke University.

title: The DNA dilemma
summary: What would you do if a company sold your genetic data? We designed a classroom discussion around four people with different stakes in that decision.
role: Tonantzin Real Rojas and I designed the scenarios and led the class discussion together. The web implementation was built with Gemini assistance, as credited in the repository.
question: A consumer, company executive, buyer, and data scientist might see the same genetic-data sale very differently. We wanted classmates to work through those perspectives and think about the responsibilities involved.
approach: Designed four stakeholder paths around a hypothetical genetic-data sale and what might follow from it.
Created branching choices about consent, privacy, research value, and responsibilities within an organization.
Added reflection prompts and a recap of each participant’s decisions for the class discussion.
takeaway: The point was to give classmates a set of decisions to work through, then a chance to discuss why they chose what they did. Taking on another role was part of that exercise.
limitation: The scenarios are hypothetical and inspired by real events. They’re teaching material for an ethics discussion, rather than a factual account or legal analysis of the 23andMe case.
credits: Discussion and scenario design: Ammy Lin and Tonantzin Real Rojas. Developed for IDS 704: Data Science Ethics and Policy at Duke University, with AI-assisted web implementation.
motif_label: Four roles in a genetic-data sale

title: Looking at patterns in happiness data
summary: Using World Happiness Report data to ask how health, economic conditions, generosity, and freedom relate to reported well-being.
question: Does the association between health and happiness vary with economic conditions? We also looked at whether generosity and freedom were related to happiness differently when considered together.
approach: Combined World Happiness Report data from 2015 to 2019 and explored country-level patterns.
Used linear regression with a life-expectancy-by-GDP interaction and country-clustered standard errors.
Fit an ordinal logistic model with a generosity-by-freedom interaction, then plotted predicted probabilities and discussed the modeling assumptions.
takeaway: The fitted associations depended on the interactions in the models. Looking at a single coefficient in isolation would have hidden that. We wrote up the analysis as a course policy memo addressed to UNDP.
limitation: This was an observational class project. Country-level associations do not establish the effects of a policy on individuals. Missing country-years, changing survey measures, and the model assumptions also limit the conclusions.
credits: Team: Arvind Kandala, Ammy Lin, Lingyue Hao, and Shelly Cao. Completed for IDS 702: Modeling and Representation of Data at Duke in Fall 2025. This repository is a fork of the team project.

title: Comparing models for mental-health text
summary: We compared sentence embeddings, topic models, and clustering for a seven-label text-classification dataset.
question: Would adding topic or cluster features improve on sentence embeddings alone? We compared those approaches using a public dataset of text labeled with mental-health-related categories.
approach: Prepared text and compared LDA topic features, TF-IDF-based clusters, and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings.
Trained logistic regression classifiers on each representation and on combinations of features.
Compared accuracy, macro F1, and per-class results on a stratified test split, including confusion matrices.
takeaway: In the saved run, sentence embeddings reached about 70% accuracy and 0.62 macro F1. Adding topic or cluster features changed those results very little. Performance varied considerably across labels, which was easier to see in the per-class metrics than in overall accuracy.
limitation: These are dataset labels, not clinical diagnoses, and the project is not a diagnostic tool. Some unsupervised features were fitted before the train/test split; a stricter comparison would fit those steps on training data only. Class imbalance and the source of the text also matter when interpreting the results.
credits: Team: Jordan Andrew, Aesha Gandhi, and Ammy Lin. Completed in December 2025. This repository is a fork of the collaborative project.
image_alt: Confusion matrix for the sentence-embedding baseline, showing predictions across seven dataset labels
image_caption: The saved notebook’s sentence-embedding baseline confusion matrix, labeled “BERT Only Model” in the source.

title: Primes and quadratic forms
summary: Python tools that accompany our math comps paper, including reduction, enumeration, and composition of binary quadratic forms.
question: How can computation help us explore binary quadratic forms and the ideas in our paper, Primes and Quadratic Forms?
approach: Implemented routines to reduce binary quadratic forms and list reduced forms of a given negative discriminant.
Included checks for fundamental discriminants and tools for enumerating forms across a range of discriminants.
Computed Dirichlet composition and supplied examples that call the routines.
takeaway: The code gives readers a way to work through concrete examples alongside the paper, including the reduced forms for a discriminant and the results of composing forms.
limitation: The routines focus on the examples in our mathematics paper. The repository does not include large-input benchmarks.
credits: Paper and accompanying code: Sophie Boileau, Alejandro González Argüelles, Grace Hanson, Ammy Lin, and Hugh Shanno. This repository is a fork of the collaborative comps project.

title: Teaching reproducible Python workflows
summary: An introductory demo I prepared as a data engineering TA, covering virtual environments, testing, Makefiles, Docker, and GitHub Actions.
role: I prepared the demo for my role as a teaching assistant for IDS 706: Data Engineering Systems.
question: How can a small Python example help students practice the tools around their code? The program itself prints a welcome message, leaving room to focus on setup, tests, containers, and automation.
approach: Kept the Python application small and added a test suite and Makefile.
Included a Dockerfile and a GitHub Actions testing workflow, with setup instructions for different operating systems.
Published an accompanying web demo. A separate containerization example uses a city-weather analysis to demonstrate a reproducible project structure.
takeaway: The materials give students a small project to work through while learning how to test and run their code consistently. The repository includes the setup instructions and example files.
limitation: This is an introductory exercise. The application is intentionally small so students can concentrate on setup, tests, containers, and automation.
credits: Teaching demo prepared by Ammy Lin for IDS 706 at Duke University.
motif_label: A small project for practicing the workflow
